::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="probability normal student-t chi-squared" data-difficulty="3"}
## Deriving the Student-$t$ distribution

Let $X_1,\ldots, X_n \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$. From @prp-normal-sample-mean and @prp-normal-sample-variance, we saw that

1. $\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$,
2. $\dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \;\sim\; \chi^2_{\,n-1}$, and
3. The sample variance $S^2$ was independent of the sample mean $\bar{X}$.

Derive the PDF of the random variable
$$
T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S / \sqrt{n}}.
$$

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

Set 
$$
Z \;=\; \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), 
\qquad 
U \;=\; \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{\,n-1},
$$
with $Z$ independent of $U$. Then
$$
T \;=\; \frac{\sigma Z}{\sqrt{(\sigma^2 U)/(n-1)}} \;=\; \frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/\nu}},
\qquad \nu := n-1.
$$

**Conditional distribution.** Conditioning on $U=u$,
$$
T \mid U=u \;=\; \frac{Z}{\sqrt{u/\nu}}
\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\; \frac{\nu}{u}\right),
$$
so its conditional density is
$$
f_{T\mid U}(t\mid u)
= \sqrt{\frac{u}{2\pi\nu}}\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{u}{2\nu}t^2\right), \qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

**Mixture over $U$.** The marginal PDF of $T$ is
$$
f_T(t) 
= \int_0^\infty f_{T\mid U}(t\mid u)\, f_U(u)\, \mathrm{d}u,
$$

where $f_U(u) = \dfrac{1}{2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)}\,u^{\nu/2-1} e^{-u/2}$ for $u>0$. Thus

\begin{align*}
f_T(t)
&= \int_0^\infty 
\left[\sqrt{\frac{u}{2\pi\nu}}\;e^{-\frac{u}{2\nu}t^2}\right]
\left[\frac{1}{2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)}\,u^{\nu/2-1} e^{-u/2}\right] \mathrm{d}u \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\nu}\,2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)}
\int_0^\infty 
u^{\frac{\nu+1}{2}-1}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\!\left(1+\frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)u\right\}
\,\mathrm{d}u.
\end{align*}

Use the Gamma integral $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty u^{a-1} e^{-b u}\,\mathrm{d}u = \Gamma(a)\,b^{-a}$ with
$a=\frac{\nu+1}{2}$ and $b=\frac{1}{2}\!\left(1+\frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)$:

\begin{align*}
f_T(t)
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\nu}\,2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)}
\cdot \Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)
\left[\frac{1}{2}\!\left(1+\frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)\right]^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}} \\
&= \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)}
\left(1+\frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}, \qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\end{align*}

This is the **Student-$t$** density with $\nu=n-1$ degrees of freedom:
$$
T \sim t_\nu \quad \text{with} \quad
f_T(t) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)}
\left(1+\frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}.
$$


</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="statistics" data-difficulty="0"}
## Sample Mean and Standard Deviation

Emergency admissions to $10$ hospitals were recorded on a particular day.  

The summary statistics were:

- $n = 10$  
- $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 207$  
- $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 4501$

Find the **sample mean** $\bar{x}$ and the **sample standard deviation** $s$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

The sample mean is
$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = \frac{207}{10} = 20.7.
$$

To find the sample variance,
$$
s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n \bar{x}^2\right).
$$

Substituting the values:
$$
s^2 = \frac{1}{9}\left(4501 - 10 \times (20.7)^2\right)
= \frac{1}{9}(4501 - 4284.9)
= 24.011.
$$

Taking the square root gives the sample standard deviation:
$$
s = \sqrt{24.011} \approx 4.900.
$$

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="clt probability" data-difficulty="1" #q-clt-approx1}
## Central Limit Theorem Approximation

The scores that responders give on a questionnaire can be assumed to be independent random variables, each with the following probability distribution:

| Score | 1   | 2   | 3   | 4   | 5   |
|:-------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| Probability | 0.3 | 0.1 | 0.2 | 0.1 | 0.3 |

Use the <span class="xref-no-num">[Central Limit Theorem @thm-clt]</span> to approximate the probability that the average score from $n = 100$ responders lies in the range $(2.8,\,3.2)$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

Let $X$ be the score for a randomly selected responder.  
We first compute the moments.

**Expected value:**
$$
\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^5 i \Pr(X=i)
= 1(0.3) + 2(0.1) + 3(0.2) + 4(0.1) + 5(0.3) = 3.
$$

**Second moment:**
$$
\mathrm{E}[X^2] = \sum_{i=1}^5 i^2 \Pr(X=i)
= 1^2(0.3) + 2^2(0.1) + 3^2(0.2) + 4^2(0.1) + 5^2(0.3) = 11.6.
$$

**Variance:**
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathrm{E}[X^2] - (\mathrm{E}[X])^2 = 11.6 - 9 = 2.6.
$$

---

Let $\bar{X}$ be the sample mean. By the Central Limit Theorem,
$$
\bar{X} \overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\!\left(3,\; \frac{2.6}{100}\right).
$$

We want:
$$
\Pr(2.8 < \bar{X} < 3.2)
= \Pr\!\left(\frac{2.8-3}{\sqrt{2.6/100}} < Z < \frac{3.2-3}{\sqrt{2.6/100}}\right),
$$
where $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

Compute the bounds:
$$
\frac{2.8-3}{\sqrt{0.026}} = -1.24, 
\qquad
\frac{3.2-3}{\sqrt{0.026}} = 1.24.
$$

Thus,
$$
\Pr(-1.24 < Z < 1.24) 
= \Pr(Z < 1.24) - \Pr(Z < -1.24).
$$

Using R, Python or referring to the standard normal tables:
$$
\Pr(Z < 1.24) = 0.8925, \qquad \Pr(Z < -1.24) = 0.1075.
$$

So,
$$
\Pr(2.8 < \bar{X} < 3.2) \approx 0.8925 - 0.1075 = 0.785.
$$

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="clt binomial" data-difficulty="1" #q-binom-clt}
## Normal Approximation to the Binomial

Use the <span class="xref-no-num">[Central Limit Theorem @thm-clt]</span> to justify the Normal approximation to the <span class="xref-no-num">[Binomial @sec-binom]</span>.  

That is, if $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, show that for large $n$ (with $p \neq 0,1$),
$$
X \overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N} \big(np,\; np(1-p)\big).
$$

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

The Binomial distribution counts the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials.

For trial $i$, define the indicator
$$
I_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if success}, \\
0, & \text{if failure}.
\end{cases}
$$

Each $I_i$ has
$$
\mathrm{E}[I_i] = p, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(I_i) = p(1-p).
$$

The total number of successes is
$$
X = \sum_{i=1}^n I_i.
$$

By the Central Limit Theorem, the sum of independent, identically distributed random variables is approximately Normal when $n$ is large. Therefore,
$$
X \overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N} \big(np,\; np(1-p)\big).
$$

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="estimator bias variance" data-difficulty="1" #q-prop-of-estimators1}
## Properties of an Estimator I

Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3$ are independent random variables, each with expectation  
$\mathrm{E}[X] = 2\theta + 1$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \theta^2/12$, where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter.  

Consider the estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$, where
$$
\hat{\theta} = 2X_1 - X_2 + X_3.
$$

Answer the following:

(a) Find the **expectation** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.  
(b) Find the **variance** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.  
(c) Determine the **bias** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a) Expectation**
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \mathrm{E}[2X_1 - X_2 + X_3] 
= 2\mathrm{E}[X_1] - \mathrm{E}[X_2] + \mathrm{E}[X_3].
$$
Since each $X_i$ has the same mean $\mathrm{E}[X] = 2\theta + 1$,
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] = 2(2\theta+1) - (2\theta+1) + (2\theta+1) = 4\theta + 2.
$$

---

**(b) Variance**
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = \operatorname{Var}(2X_1 - X_2 + X_3).
$$
Since the $X_i$ are independent,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = 4\operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{Var}(X_2) + \operatorname{Var}(X_3).
$$
Each has variance $\theta^2/12$, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = (4+1+1)\frac{\theta^2}{12} = \frac{\theta^2}{2}.
$$

---

**(c) Bias**
$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta = (4\theta + 2) - \theta = 3\theta + 2.
$$

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="estimation bias variance" data-difficulty="1" #q-prop-of-estimators2}
## Properties of an Estimator II

Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4$ are independent random variables, each with  
$\mathrm{E}[X] = 3\theta$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \theta^2/9$, where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter.  

Consider the estimator
$$
\hat{\theta} = X_1 + 2X_2 - X_3 + X_4.
$$

Answer the following:

(a) Find the **expectation** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.  
(b) Find the **variance** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.  
(c) Determine the **bias** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a) Expectation**
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] + 2\mathrm{E}[X_2] - \mathrm{E}[X_3] + \mathrm{E}[X_4].
$$
Each has mean $3\theta$, so
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] = 3\theta + 2(3\theta) - 3\theta + 3\theta = 9\theta.
$$

---

**(b) Variance**
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + 4\operatorname{Var}(X_2) + \operatorname{Var}(X_3) + \operatorname{Var}(X_4).
$$
Each has variance $\theta^2/9$, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = (1+4+1+1)\frac{\theta^2}{9} = \frac{7\theta^2}{9}.
$$

---

**(c) Bias**
$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta = 9\theta - \theta = 8\theta.
$$

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="estimator bias variance expectation" data-difficulty="1" #q-prop-of-estimators3}

## Properties of an Estimator III

Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3$ are independent random variables, each with  
$$
\mathrm{E}[X_i] = \theta - 5, 
\qquad 
\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = 2\theta^2,
$$
where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter.  

Consider the estimator
$$
\hat{\theta} = X_1 + 2X_2 - 4X_3.
$$

Answer the following:

(a) Find the **expectation** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.  
(b) Find the **variance** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.  
(c) Determine the **bias** of the estimator $\hat{\theta}$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**(a) Expectation**

Using linearity of expectation:
$$
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]
= \mathrm{E}[X_1] + 2\,\mathrm{E}[X_2] - 4\,\mathrm{E}[X_3]
= (\theta - 5) + 2(\theta - 5) - 4(\theta - 5)
= -\,(\theta - 5)
= 5 - \theta.
$$

---

**(b) Variance**

Because $X_1, X_2, X_3$ are independent,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})
= \mathrm{Var}(X_1) + 4\,\mathrm{Var}(X_2) + 16\,\mathrm{Var}(X_3)
= (1 + 4 + 16)\,2\theta^2
= 42\theta^2.
$$

---

**(c) Bias**

The bias is
$$
\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})
= \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta
= (5 - \theta) - \theta
= 5 - 2\theta.
$$

Hence the estimator is **biased**, and the bias depends linearly on $\theta$.

</details>

:::



::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="poisson estimator bias variance" data-difficulty="1" #q-prop-poisson}
## Properties of the Poisson distribution

A hospital records the **number of patients arriving at the emergency department per hour**.  

Suppose $X \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, where $\lambda$ is the (unknown) mean arrival rate.

1. Compute $\mathrm{E}[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
2. We estimate $\lambda$ by the **sample mean** $\hat{\lambda} = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ from $n$ independent hours of observation.  
   Show that $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\lambda}] = \lambda$ and compute $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\lambda})$.
3. Suppose in one hour you observe $x=7$ arrivals.  
   
   (i) Compute the estimate $\hat{\lambda}_{\text{obs}}$.  
   (ii) Using $\hat{\lambda}_{\text{obs}}$ as $\lambda$, compute the pmf value $p(X=7 \mid \hat{\lambda}_{\text{obs}})$.  
   (iii) Compute $F(7 \mid \lambda = \hat{\lambda}_\text{obs} = \mathrm{Pr}(X \leq 7 \mid \hat{\lambda}_\text{\text{obs}})$ using $\hat{\lambda}_{\text{obs}}$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

1. For $X \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$,
   $$
   \mathrm{E}[X] = \lambda, \quad \mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda.
   $$

2. If $\hat{\lambda} = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, then
   $$
   \mathrm{E}[\hat{\lambda}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[X_i] = \lambda,
   $$
   so $\hat{\lambda}$ is unbiased.  
   Since $\mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \lambda$ and the $X_i$ are independent,
   $$
   \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\lambda}) = \frac{\lambda}{n}.
   $$

3. With $x=7$,  
   (i) $\hat{\lambda}_{\text{obs}} = 7$.  
   (ii) The PMF value is
   $$
   \mathrm{Pr}(X=7 \mid \lambda=7) = \frac{7^7 e^{-7}}{7!}.
   $$
   (iii) The CDF value is
   $$
   \mathrm{Pr}(X \leq 7 \mid \lambda=7) = \sum_{k=0}^7 \frac{7^k e^{-7}}{k!}.
   $$

In Python:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show code"

from scipy.stats import poisson

lambd_hat = 7
part_ii = poisson.pmf(k = 7, mu=lambd_hat) # pmf value at x = 7
part_iii = poisson.cdf(k = 7, mu=lambd_hat) # cdf value at x = 7

print(f"Part (ii) answer: {part_ii} \nPart (iii) answer: {part_iii}")

```

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="estimator variance covariance" data-difficulty="2"}

## Variance of an Estimator (with dependence)

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be random variables with the **same variance** and **same pairwise covariance**:
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=\tau\quad (i\neq j),
$$
where $\sigma^2>0$ and $\tau$ are known constants (no independence is assumed).

For fixed weights $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}$, consider the linear estimator
$$
\hat{\theta}=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i.
$$

Compute $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})$ in terms of ${a_i}$, $\sigma^2$, and $\tau$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

Using $\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_i a_i X_i\right)=\sum_i\sum_j a_i a_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$ and the structure of the covariances:
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})
= \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \sigma^2 + \sum_{i\neq j} a_i a_j \tau
= \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 + \tau \left[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\Big)^2-\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right].
$$
Hence a compact form is
$$
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})=(\sigma^2-\tau)\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 + \tau\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\Big)^2.}
$$

If the $X_i$ were independent, then $\tau=0$ and we recover $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})=\sigma^2\sum_i a_i^2$.

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="consistency bias variance" data-difficulty="2" #q-prove-consistency1}

## Proving Consistency I

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ be a random sample such that each
$$
\operatorname{E}[X_i]=\mu,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2.
$$
Consider the following family of estimators of the mean $\mu$:
$$
\hat{\mu}_n = \frac{1}{n + c} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i,
$$
where $c\in\mathbb{R}$ is a constant.

Show that $\hat{\mu}_n$ is a consistent estimator of $\mu$ for all $c\in\mathbb{R}$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**Bias:** We have

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{E}[\hat{\mu}_n] &= \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{n + c} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] \\
&= \frac{1}{n+c} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[X_i] \\
&= \frac{1}{n+c} \sum_{i=1}^n \mu \\
&= \frac{n \mu }{n + c}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the bias is
$$
\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\mu}_n) = \frac{n \mu }{n + c} - \mu = \frac{n\mu}{n+c} - \frac{(n+c)\mu}{n+c} = -\frac{c \mu}{n + c}.
$$

**Variance:** Due to independence of the $X_i$, we have

\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\mu}_n] &= \mathrm{Var}\left[\frac{1}{n + c} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] \\
&= \frac{1}{(n+c)^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}[X_i] \\
&= \frac{1}{(n+c)^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma^2 \\
&= \frac{n \sigma^2 }{(n + c)^2}.
\end{align*}

**Consistency:** To show consistency, we use @prp-sufficient-consistency. From the computed bias, we have (for any value of $c\in\mathbb{R}$):
$$
\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\mu}_n) = -\frac{c \mu}{n + c} \rightarrow 0, \quad \text{as } n\rightarrow \infty.
$$
Therefore, the estimator is *asymptotically unbiased*. Similarly, the variance converges to $0$ for all $c\in\mathbb{R}$:
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\mu}_n) = \frac{n \sigma^2 }{(n + c)^2} \rightarrow 0, \quad \text{as } n\rightarrow \infty.
$$
Therefore, $\hat{\mu}_n$ is a consistent estimator of $\mu$ for all $c\in\mathbb{R}$.

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="likelihood geometric" data-difficulty="1" #q-geom-likelihood}

## Computing Likelihoods I

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Geometric}(p)$ be a random sample.

Derive the **likelihood function**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

For independent and identically distributed data, the <span class="xref-no-num">[likelihood function @def-likelihood]</span> takes the form
$$
L(p ; \underline{x}) = f(\underline{x} \mid p) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid p),
$$
where $f(x_i\mid p)$ is PMF of the <span class="xref-no-num">[geometric distribution @sec-geom]</span>:
$$
f(x_i \mid p) = p(1-p)^{x_i - 1}.
$$
Therefore, the likelihood takes the form
\begin{align*}
L(p; \underline{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(1-p)^{x_i - 1} \\
&= p(1-p)^{x_1-1}\times p(1-p)^{x_2-1}\times \ldots \times p(1-p)^{x_n-1} \\
&= p^n(1-p)^{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - 1)} \\
&= p^n(1-p)^{n(\bar{x} - 1)},
\end{align*}
where $\bar{x}$ is the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample mean @def-sample-mean]</span>.
</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="likelihood normal" data-difficulty="1" #q-normal-var-likelihood}

## Computing Likelihoods II

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ be a random sample.

Derive the **likelihood function**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

For independent and identically distributed data, the <span class="xref-no-num">[likelihood function @def-likelihood]</span> takes the form
$$
L(\mu ; \underline{x}) = f(\underline{x} \mid \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \mu),
$$
where $f(x_i\mid \mu)$ is PDF of the <span class="xref-no-num">[normal distribution @sec-normal]</span> (with variance $\sigma^2=1$):
$$
f(x_i \mid \mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2} \right\}.
$$
Therefore, the likelihood takes the form
\begin{align*}
L(\mu; \underline{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2} \right\} \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{(x_1 - \mu)^2}{2} \right\} \times \ldots \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left\{ -\frac{(x_n - \mu)^2}{2} \right\} \\
&= (2\pi)^{-n/2} \exp\left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n -\frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2}  \right\} \\
&= (2\pi)^{-n/2} \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{2 }\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2 \right\}.
\end{align*}
</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="likelihood log-normal" data-difficulty="1" #q-lognormal-likelihood}

## Computing Likelihoods III

Suppose we have $n$ i.i.d. <span class="xref-no-num">[log normal @sec-lognormal]</span> observations
$$
X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{LogNormal}(\mu, \gamma).
$$

Derive the **likelihood function**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

For independent and identically distributed data, the <span class="xref-no-num">[likelihood function @def-likelihood]</span> takes the form
$$
L(\mu, \gamma ; \underline{x}) = f(\underline{x} \mid \mu, \gamma) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \mu, \gamma),
$$
where $f(x_i\mid \mu, \gamma)$ is PDF of the <span class="xref-no-num">[log normal distribution @sec-lognormal]</span> (with $\sigma^2 = \gamma$):
$$
f(x_i \mid \mu, \gamma) = \frac{1}{x_i\sqrt{2\pi\gamma}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\log(x_i)-\mu)^2}{2\gamma}\right).
$$
Therefore, the likelihood takes the form
$$
\begin{align*}
L(\mu, \gamma; \underline{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{x_i\sqrt{2\pi\gamma}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\log(x_i)-\mu)^2}{2\gamma}\right) \\
&= (2\pi\gamma)^{-n/2} \exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n (\log(x_i) - \mu)^2\right\} \left(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\right)^{-1}.
\end{align*}
$$

</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="fisher-information binomial" data-difficulty="2" #q-fisher-info-binomial}

## Fisher Information for a Binomial Observation

Suppose we have a single <span class="xref-no-num">[Binomial @sec-binom]</span> observation:
$$
X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, \theta),
$$
Derive the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span> and the <span class="xref-no-num">[observed Fisher information @def-observed-fisher]</span>.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

Note: We want to compute $\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2} \ell(\theta; X)\right]$ for the Fisher information and $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ for the observed Fisher information.

**Step 1: Compute log-likelihood**

Since we have a single observation, the likelihood is just the Binomial PMF:
$$
L(\theta ; x) = \binom{n}{x} \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}.
$$
Therefore, the log-likelihood takes the form
$$
\ell(\theta; x) = \log L(\theta ; x) = \log\left(\binom{n}{x}\right) + x \log \theta + (n-x)\log(1-\theta).
$$

**Step 2: Compute Derivatives**

We compute the first and second derivatives of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$:
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta; x) &= \frac{x}{\theta} - \frac{n-x}{1-\theta} \\
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta; x) &= -\frac{x}{\theta^2} - \frac{n-x}{(1-\theta)^2}.
\end{align*}

**Step 3: Compute Fisher Information**

We have
$$
\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2} \ell(\theta; X)\right] = -\mathrm{E}\left[-\frac{X}{\theta^2} - \frac{n-X}{(1-\theta)^2}\right],
$$
where the **random** component of the expectation is $X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n, \theta)$. Therefore, manipulating the expectation:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}(\theta) &= \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{X}{\theta^2} + \frac{n-X}{(1-\theta)^2}\right] \\
&= \frac{1}{\theta^2}\mathrm{E}[X] + \frac{1}{(1-\theta)^2} \mathrm{E}[n - X] \\
&= \frac{n\theta}{\theta^2} + \frac{n - n\theta}{(1-\theta)^2},
\end{align*}
using the fact that $\mathrm{E}[X] = n\theta$. Continuing:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}(\theta) &= \frac{n}{\theta} + \frac{n}{1-\theta} \\
&= \frac{n(1-\theta) + n\theta}{\theta(1-\theta)} \\
&= \frac{n}{\theta(1-\theta)}.
\end{align*}

**Step 4: Compute MLE**

We require the MLE for the observed Fisher information. We solve:
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta; x) &= 0 \\
\frac{x}{\theta} - \frac{n-x}{1-\theta} &= 0 \\
x(1-\theta) &= \theta(n-x) \\
x &= n\theta \\
\Rightarrow \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} &= \frac{x}{n}.
\end{align*}

**Step 5: Compute observed Fisher information**

Given the MLE $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \frac{x}{n}$ and the derived Fisher information, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) &=  \frac{n}{\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}(1-\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}})} \\
&= \frac{n}{x/n(1-x/n)} \\
&= \frac{n^3}{x(n - x)}.
\end{align*}

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="fisher-information geometric" data-difficulty="2" #q-fisher-info-geometric}

## Fisher Information for Geometric Data

Suppose we have a random <span class="xref-no-num">[Geometric @sec-geom]</span> sample:
$$
X_1,\ldots, X_n \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Geom}(\theta).
$$
Derive the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span> and the <span class="xref-no-num">[observed Fisher information @def-observed-fisher]</span> for both a **single observation** and the **whole random sample**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

Since we have i.i.d. observations, we can use @prp-fisher-one-obs to compute the Fisher information for the **whole random sample** by computing $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)$ for a single observation. However, the observed information requires the MLE using all $n$ data points $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. So, let's compute $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)$ using the **whole sample** $X_1,\ldots, X_n$:

**Step 1: Compute log-likelihood**

For i.i.d. Geometric data, we have
\begin{align*}
L(\theta; \underline{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \theta(1-\theta)^{x_i - 1} \\
&= \theta^n(1-\theta)^{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - 1)} \\
&= \theta^n(1-\theta)^{n(\bar{x} - 1)}.
\end{align*}
Therefore, the log-likelihood takes the form
$$
\ell(\theta; \underline{x}) = \log L(\theta ; \underline{x}) = n\log(\theta) + n(\bar{x}-1)\log(1-\theta).
$$

**Step 2: Compute Derivatives**

We compute the first and second derivatives of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$:
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta; \underline{x}) &= \frac{n}{\theta} - \frac{n(\bar{x} - 1)}{1-\theta} \\
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ell(\theta; \underline{x}) &= -\frac{n}{\theta^2} - \frac{n(\bar{x} - 1)}{(1-\theta)^2}.
\end{align*}

**Step 3: Compute Fisher Information**

We have
$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = -\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2} \ell(\theta; \underline{X})\right] = -\mathrm{E}\left[-\frac{n}{\theta^2} - \frac{n(\bar{X} - 1)}{(1-\theta)^2}\right],
$$
where the **random** component of the expectation is $X_i\sim\mathrm{Geom}(\theta)$. Therefore, manipulating the expectation:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) &= \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{n}{\theta^2} + \frac{n(\bar{X} - 1)}{(1-\theta)^2}\right] \\
&= \frac{n}{\theta^2} + \frac{n}{(1-\theta)^2} \mathrm{E}[\bar{X}] - \frac{n}{(1-\theta)^2} \\
&= \frac{n}{\theta^2} + \frac{n}{(1-\theta)^2} \frac{1}{\theta} - \frac{n}{(1-\theta)^2},
\end{align*}
where we used the fact that 
$$
\mathrm{E}[\bar{X}] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[X_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta} = \frac{1}{\theta},
$$
and $\mathrm{E}[X_i] = \tfrac{1}{\theta}$. Continuing:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) &= \frac{n (1-\theta)^2}{\theta^2(1-\theta)^2} + \frac{n\theta}{\theta^2(1-\theta)^2}  - \frac{n\theta^2}{\theta^2(1-\theta)^2}\\
&= \frac{n(1-\theta) +n\theta}{\theta^2(1-\theta)} \\
&= \frac{n}{\theta^2(1-\theta)}.
\end{align*}
This immediately implies the Fisher information for a single observation is
$$
\mathcal{I}_1(\theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^2(1-\theta)}.
$$

**Step 4: Compute MLE**

We require the MLE for the observed Fisher information. We solve:
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \ell(\theta; \underline{x}) &= 0 \\
\frac{n}{\theta} - \frac{n(\bar{x} - 1)}{1-\theta} &= 0 \\
n(1-\theta) &= n \theta (\bar{x} - 1) \\
1 &= \theta \bar{x} \\
\Rightarrow \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} &= \frac{1}{\bar{x}}.
\end{align*}

**Step 5: Compute observed Fisher information**

Given the MLE $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \frac{1}{\bar{x}}$ and the derived Fisher information, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) &=  \frac{n}{\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2(1-\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}})} \\
&= \frac{n}{\bar{x}^{-2}(1-\bar{x}^{-1})}. \\
&= \frac{n \bar{x}^3}{\bar{x} - 1}.
\end{align*}
This immediately implies the observed Fisher information for a single observation is
$$
\mathcal{I}_1(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) = \frac{\bar{x}^3}{\bar{x} - 1}.
$$

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="fisher-information normal" data-difficulty="2" #q-fisher-info-var-normal}

## Fisher Information of the Variance of Normal Data

Suppose we have a random <span class="xref-no-num">[Normal @sec-normal]</span> sample:
$$
X_1,\ldots, X_n \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma),
$$
where $\mu$ is a *known* value $\gamma$ is *unknown*.

Derive the <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span> and the <span class="xref-no-num">[observed Fisher information @def-observed-fisher]</span> of $\gamma$ for the **whole random sample**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

Note: We want to compute $\mathcal{I}(\gamma) = -\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\gamma^2} \ell(\gamma; \underline{X})\right]$ for the Fisher information and $\hat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ for the observed Fisher information.

**Step 1: Compute log-likelihood**

Since we have $n$ i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma)$ with $\mu$ known, the likelihood function is
$$
\begin{align*}
L(\gamma;\underline{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\gamma}} \exp\left\{-\frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\gamma}\right\} \\
&= (2 \pi)^{-n/2} \gamma^{-n/2} \exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2\right\}.
\end{align*}
$$
Therefore, the log-likelihood takes the form
$$
\ell(\gamma; \underline{x}) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log(\gamma) - \frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2.
$$

**Step 2: Compute Derivatives**

We compute the first and second derivatives of the log-likelihood with respect to $\gamma$:
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \gamma} \ell(\gamma; \underline{x}) &= -\frac{n}{2\gamma} + \frac{1}{2\gamma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2,  \\
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \gamma^2} \ell(\gamma; \underline{x}) &= \frac{n}{2\gamma^2} - \frac{1}{\gamma^3}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2.
\end{align*}
$$
**Step 3: Compute Fisher Information**

We have
$$
\mathcal{I}(\gamma) = -\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\gamma^2} \ell(\gamma; \underline{X})\right] = -\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{n}{2\gamma^2} - \frac{1}{\gamma^3}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2\right],
$$
where the **random** component of the expectation is the *random data* $X_i\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma)$. Therefore, manipulating the expectation:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}(\gamma) &=  -\frac{n}{2\gamma^2} + \frac{1}{\gamma^3}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[(X_i - \mu)^2] \\
&= -\frac{n}{2\gamma^2} + \frac{1}{\gamma^3}\sum_{i=1}^n \gamma,
\end{align*}
$$
using the fact that each $X_i - \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \gamma)$ and so $\mathrm{E}[(X_i - \mu)^2] = \mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \gamma$. Continuing:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}(\gamma) &= -\frac{n}{2\gamma^2} + \frac{n\gamma}{\gamma^3} \\
&= \frac{n}{2\gamma^2}
\end{align*}
$$

**Step 4: Compute MLE**

We require the MLE for the observed Fisher information. We solve:
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \gamma} \ell(\gamma; \underline{x}) &= 0 \\
-\frac{n}{2\gamma} + \frac{1}{2\gamma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2 &= 0 \\
\Rightarrow \hat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{MLE}} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2 
\end{align*}
$$

**Step 5: Compute observed Fisher information**

Given the MLE $\hat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2 $ and the derived Fisher information, we have
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{I}(\hat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{MLE}}) &= \frac{n}{2\hat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{MLE}}^2} \\
&= \frac{n^3}{2\left(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2\right)^2}.
\end{align*}
$$

</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="bayes asymptotic-posterior exam-style" data-difficulty="2" #q-asymp-post-variance}

## Asymptotic Posterior for the Variance Parameter

Suppose we have an independent and identically distributed sample
$$
\underline{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)^\top
$$
from a distribution with PDF
$$
f(x \mid \gamma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \gamma}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{x^2}{2\gamma}\right], 
\qquad \gamma > 0.
$$

Determine the **asymptotic posterior distribution** for $\gamma$.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

**Step 1: Likelihood**

$$
f(\underline{x} \mid \gamma)
= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \gamma}} 
   \exp\!\left[-\frac{x_i^2}{2\gamma}\right]
= (2\pi \gamma)^{-n/2} 
  \exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right].
$$

**Step 2: Log-likelihood**

$$
\ell(\gamma; \underline{x})
= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) 
  - \frac{n}{2}\log(\gamma) 
  - \frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2.
$$

**Step 3: Derivatives**

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \gamma}
= -\frac{n}{2\gamma} 
  + \frac{1}{2\gamma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2,
$$

$$
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \gamma^2}
= \frac{n}{2\gamma^2} 
  - \frac{1}{\gamma^3}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2.
$$

Let  
$$
a = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2.
$$

**Step 4: MLE**

Solving $\partial \ell / \partial \gamma = 0$:

$$
-\frac{n}{2\gamma} + \frac{a}{2\gamma^2} = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\hat{\gamma} = \frac{a}{n} 
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2.
$$

**Step 5: Fisher Information**

For one observation:

$$
\ell(\gamma)
= -\tfrac12\log(2\pi\gamma) 
  - \tfrac{x^2}{2\gamma},
$$
and so
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \gamma^2}
= \frac{1}{2\gamma^2} - \frac{x^2}{\gamma^3}.
$$

Taking expectation under $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\gamma)$:

$$
\mathcal{I}(\gamma) 
= -\mathrm{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \gamma^2}\right]
= -\left(\frac{1}{2\gamma^2} - \frac{\gamma}{\gamma^3}\right)
= \frac{1}{2\gamma^2}.
$$

Thus for $n$ observations:

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\gamma) = \frac{n}{2\gamma^2}.
$$

Evaluated at the MLE:

$$
\mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\gamma}) 
= \frac{n}{2\hat{\gamma}^2}.
$$

**Step 6: Asymptotic posterior**

By @thm-bernstein-von-mises

$$
\gamma \mid \underline{x}
\approx 
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\hat{\gamma},\;
I_n(\hat{\gamma})^{-1}
\right)
=
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\hat{\gamma},\;
\frac{2\hat{\gamma}^2}{n}
\right).
$$

That is,

$$
\boxed{
\gamma \mid \underline{x}
\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} 
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2,\;
\frac{2}{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)^2
\right).
}
$$


</details>

:::


::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="bayes asymptotic-posterior poisson" data-difficulty="2" #q-asymp-post-poisson}

## Asymptotic Posterior for Poisson Data

Suppose we have independent <span class="xref-no-num">[Poisson @sec-pois]</span> observations
$$
X_1,\ldots, X_n \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)
$$

1. Determine the general <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic posterior distribution @thm-bernstein-von-mises]</span> for $\lambda$.
2. Suppose we observe $n = 100$ data points with sample mean
   $$
   \bar{x} = 3.21.
   $$
   Compute the **asymptotic posterior distribution**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

1. **General Asymptotic Posterior.**
   1. **Log-Likelihood:** Since each observation is independent $X_i \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)$, we have
      $$
      \begin{align*}
       f(\underline{x} \mid \lambda) &= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{\lambda^{x_i} e^{-\lambda}}{x_i!} \\
       &= \lambda^{n\bar{x}} e^{-n\lambda} \left(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i! \right)^{-1}.
      \end{align*}
      $$
      Therefore, the log-likelihood is
      $$
      \log f(\underline{x} \mid \lambda) = n\bar{x} \log(\lambda) - n\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^n \log(x_i!).
      $$
    2. **Derivatives:** The derivatives of the log-likelihood are
      $$
      \begin{align*}
       \frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda} \log f(\underline{x} \mid \lambda) &= \frac{n\bar{x}}{\lambda} - n \\
       \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \lambda^2} \log f(\underline{x} \mid \lambda) &= -\frac{n\bar{x}}{\lambda^2}.
      \end{align*}
      $$
    3. **MLE:** Solving
      $$
      \frac{n\bar{x}}{\lambda} - n = 0
      $$
      yields the maximum likelihood estimator
      $$
      \hat{\lambda} = \bar{X}.
      $$
    4. **Fisher Information:** The <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span> for the **whole sample** is thus
      $$
      \begin{align*}
       \mathcal{I}_n(\lambda) &= -\mathrm{E}\left[-\frac{n\bar{X}}{\lambda^2}\right] \\
       &= \frac{n}{n\lambda^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{E}\left[X_i\right] \\
       &= \frac{n}{\lambda},
      \end{align*}
      $$ 
      since each $\mathrm{E}[X_i] = \lambda$.
    4. **Plugging in MLE:** The <span class="xref-no-num">[observed Fisher information @def-observed-fisher]</span> is thus
      $$
      \mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\lambda}) = \frac{n}{\bar{x}}.
      $$
    5. **Asymptotic Posterior Distribution:** The <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic posterior distribution @thm-bernstein-von-mises]</span> is thus
      $$
      \lambda \mid \underline{x} \overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\left(\bar{x}, \frac{\bar{x}}{n}\right)
      $$
2. **Plug in data.**
   Using the derived result from the first part and the provided summaries of the data $n = 100$ and $\bar{x} = 3.21$, we have
   $$
   \lambda \mid \underline{x} \overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\left(3.21, 0.0321\right)
   $$
</details>

:::

::: {.callout-important .question appearance="minimal" data-tags="bayes asymptotic-posterior exponential" data-difficulty="2" #q-asymp-post-exponential}

## Asymptotic Posterior for Exponential Data

Suppose we have independent Exponential observations with rate parameter $\lambda$:
$$
X_1,\ldots,X_n \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda).
$$

1. Determine the general <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic posterior distribution @thm-bernstein-von-mises]</span> for $\lambda$.
2. Suppose we observe $n = 200$ data points with sample mean
   $$
   \bar{x} = 7.14.
   $$
   Compute the **asymptotic posterior distribution**.

<details class="solution">
  <summary>Solution</summary>

1. **General Asymptotic Posterior**

   1. **Likelihood and log-likelihood**

   The density of each $X_i$ is
   $$
   f(x_i \mid \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i}.
   $$

   Thus the likelihood is
   $$
   f(\underline{x} \mid \lambda) 
   = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i}
   = \lambda^n \exp\!\left(-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right).
   $$

   The log-likelihood is
   $$
   \ell(\lambda; \underline{x})
   = n\log\lambda - \lambda\sum_{i=1}^n x_i
   = n\log\lambda - n\lambda \bar{x}.
   $$

   2. **Derivatives**

   $$
   \frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda} \ell(\lambda; \underline{x})
   = \frac{n}{\lambda} - n\bar{x},
   \qquad
   \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \lambda^2} \ell(\lambda; \underline{x})
   = -\frac{n}{\lambda^2}.
   $$

   3. **MLE**

   Solve
   $$
   \frac{n}{\lambda} - n\bar{x} = 0,
   $$
   which gives the maximum likelihood estimator
   $$
   \hat{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\bar{X}}.
   $$

   4. **Fisher information**

   The <span class="xref-no-num">[Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span> for the **whole sample** is thus
   $$
   \mathcal{I}_n(\lambda) = -\mathrm{E}\left[-\frac{n}{\lambda^2}\right] = \frac{n}{\lambda^2}.
   $$

   Evaluated at the MLE, the <span class="xref-no-num">[observed Fisher information @def-observed-fisher]</span> is
   $$
   \mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\lambda})
   = \frac{n}{\hat{\lambda}^2}
   = n\bar{x}^2.
   $$

   5. **Asymptotic posterior distribution**

   By @thm-bernstein-von-mises
   $$
   \lambda \mid \underline{x}
   \overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\!\left(
     \hat{\lambda},\;
     \mathcal{I}_n(\hat{\lambda})^{-1}
   \right)
   = \mathcal{N}\!\left(
     \frac{1}{\bar{x}},\;
     \frac{1}{n\bar{x}^{2}}
   \right).
   $$

2. **Plugging in data**

   For $n = 200$ and $\bar{x} =  7.14$,
   $$
   \hat{\lambda} = \frac{1}{ 7.14} \approx 0.14,
   $$
   and the variance is
   $$
   \frac{1}{n\bar{x}^2}
   = \frac{1}{200 \cdot 7.14^2}
   \approx 9.807 \times 10^{-5}.
   $$

   Thus the asymptotic posterior is
   $$
   \lambda \mid \underline{x}
   \approx 
   \mathcal{N}\!\left(0.14,\; 9.807 \times 10^{-5}\right).
   $$

</details>

:::
